title: Globular Cluster, M15
caption: The globular cluster M15, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This image shows M15, also cataloged as NGC 7078, a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus that is estimated to hold more than 100,000 stars. Faint stars are recorded without the bright center burning out to white.
That balance shows what the new Mosaic 1.1 detectors could do. They could pick up faint stars without overexposing, or saturating, the bright heart of the cluster.

Hidden in the cluster is a planetary nebula called Pease 1. It appears blue and just slightly larger than a star, a small challenge for anyone scanning the image. A planetary nebula is a shell of gas thrown off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life, glowing because the hot core left behind lights it up. Finding one inside a globular cluster, a dense ball of old stars, shows that its stars are still evolving.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed M15 through B, V and I filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
filters: 436 nm · Optical B (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
537 nm · Optical V (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)

understand.eye: The I filter reaches toward near-infrared light the eye barely senses, and the detectors capture a range from faint outer stars to the bright core that the eye cannot take in at once.

explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is oriented with north to the left and east at the bottom.
alt: A dense ball of stars with a bright center, containing a tiny blue nebula slightly larger than a star.
